topic: AI and the future of work
blurb: What the evidence really says about AI and jobs, the skills that get more valuable, and the big debate about the economy.

steps.h: A job is a bundle of tasks
steps.p: A teacher plans lessons, marks work, talks to parents, manages a classroom. AI might help a lot with some tasks and not at all with others.

visual.caption: Some tasks are exposed to AI; others aren't.

steps.p: Automation: AI does the task instead of you. Augmentation: AI helps you do it better, and you stay in charge.
steps.analogy: A dishwasher automates; a sharper knife augments.

steps.p: A job where AI touches many tasks may change shape, become more productive, or shrink — it doesn't automatically vanish.
A 2023 study estimated about 80% of US workers have at least 10% of their tasks exposed to language models.

steps.h: What people actually use it for
steps.p: Real usage data shows coding is the top use, followed by writing, editing, analysis and learning.

cards.q: A 2023 study estimated about what share of US workers have at least 10% of their tasks exposed to language models?
cards.why: About 80%. Most jobs have some exposed tasks. Only about a fifth had half or more of their tasks exposed.

cards.statement: A job that's highly exposed to AI will disappear.
cards.why: False. Exposure means AI can affect its tasks. The job might change, grow more productive or shrink — not necessarily vanish.

options: Helps a person do the task, while the person stays in charge
cards.why: Help, not replace. Like a spell-checker or a coding assistant: you still decide what happens.

cards.title: Anthropic's Economic Index found software development was the most common use of Claude.
cards.detail: Analysing millions of anonymised conversations in early 2025, computer and maths tasks were the largest share, followed by writing and editing.

cards.q: Why do economists study AI by task rather than whole job?
options: AI affects specific tasks, and most jobs mix exposed and unexposed tasks
cards.why: That's where AI acts. Looking task by task shows what actually changes inside a job.

steps.p: A 2023 study of over 5,000 support agents found AI assistance raised productivity about 14% on average — and over 30% for the newest agents.
In a Harvard–BCG study, consultants using GPT-4 on suitable tasks did more, faster and better. On a task beyond AI's ability, they did worse.
AI is brilliant at some tasks and fails at others that seem equally hard. Use it outside its strengths and it backfires.
steps.analogy: A coastline, not a straight wall: hard to tell which side of the line a task is on.

steps.p: In METR's 2025 study, experienced open-source developers were actually about 19% slower with AI tools — while believing they were faster.
Often the least experienced: AI passes on best practices that experts already know.

cards.q: In the customer support study, who gained the most from AI help?
cards.why: Newcomers. The AI suggested responses learned from top performers, so new agents caught up faster.

cards.statement: In METR's 2025 study, experienced developers finished tasks faster with AI tools.
cards.why: False. They were about 19% slower, even though they expected and believed AI sped them up. Feelings aren't measurements.

options: Excels at some tasks and fails at others that seem equally hard
cards.why: Uneven ability. Knowing where it's strong — and checking where it isn't — is the key skill.

cards.title: Consultants using GPT-4 on suitable tasks finished 12% more tasks, 25% faster, with 40% higher quality.
cards.detail: The 2023 Harvard–BCG study of 758 consultants found the biggest gains among below-average performers.

cards.title: Measure your own productivity
cards.body: People often feel faster with AI when they aren't. A quick timing test tells you the truth.
cards.challenge: Time yourself on two similar tasks this week — one with AI, one without — and compare.

steps.p: When AI can produce ten drafts in seconds, knowing which one is good — and why — becomes the scarce skill.
AI output looks convincing even when wrong. Spotting errors takes real knowledge of the subject.
Asking the right question, with the right context, matters more than ever.
Skills you hand entirely to AI can fade. Doctors who relied on AI to spot growths got worse at spotting them alone.

steps.h: Learn with AI, not instead of
steps.p: Try first yourself, then use AI to check, explain and quiz you. Struggling before seeing the answer is how learning sticks.
steps.analogy: A personal trainer who spots you — not one who lifts the weights for you.

cards.q: Why does checking work become a more important skill as AI spreads?
options: AI output often looks convincing even when wrong, and spotting errors takes knowledge
cards.why: Convincing ≠ correct. Only someone who knows the subject can catch a fluent mistake.

cards.title: Doctors who regularly used AI to spot growths during colonoscopies got worse at spotting them without it.
cards.detail: A 2025 study in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology found detection without AI fell from about 28% to 22% after months of AI use.

cards.statement: Relying heavily on AI for a task can weaken your own ability to do it.
cards.why: True. Like a muscle, unused skills fade. Decide which skills you want to keep sharp and practise them yourself.

cards.q: What's the most effective way to learn a new skill with AI's help?
options: Try it yourself first, then use AI to explain, check and quiz you
Let AI do it every time
cards.why: Attempt first. The effort of trying is what builds memory. AI is great as a tutor, not a replacement.

cards.statement: Trying to answer a question before seeing the answer improves learning, even if you get it wrong.
cards.why: True. Called the pretesting effect: guessing first primes your brain to remember the right answer. It's why this app asks before it tells.

steps.p: Economist Daron Acemoglu estimated AI might add only around 1% to US economic output over a decade, because few tasks will be worth automating soon.
Goldman Sachs estimated generative AI could raise global GDP by about 7% over a decade. Some forecasters predict far bigger changes.
It depends how fast AI improves, how fast businesses adopt it, and how many tasks it can really do well.
Technology has destroyed many jobs but created new ones. About 60% of US workers in 2018 had job titles that didn't exist in 1940.
steps.analogy: Nobody in 1940 was a web designer or a social media manager.

steps.p: Even when things work out overall, individuals and towns can be hit hard in the meantime. How societies help people adapt matters.

cards.q: Research by David Autor found about what share of US workers in 2018 had job titles that didn't exist in 1940?
cards.why: About 60%. New technology keeps creating new kinds of work — though not always for the same people who lost the old kinds.

cards.statement: Economists broadly agree on how much AI will increase economic growth.
cards.why: False. Estimates range from about 1% to dramatic transformation. It depends on assumptions nobody can yet verify.

cards.q: Goldman Sachs' 2023 report estimated generative AI could raise global GDP by about…
cards.why: About 7% over ten years. It also estimated up to 300 million full-time jobs could be exposed to automation worldwide.

cards.title: Acemoglu's modest forecast assumed AI would profitably affect only about 5% of all tasks within a decade.
cards.detail: His argument: many exposed tasks won't be worth automating soon, and gains on hard tasks are smaller. Critics say he underestimates how fast AI is improving.

cards.title: You finished the course — teach one thing
cards.body: Explaining something is the best test of whether you understand it.
cards.challenge: Explain one idea from this course — tokens, RLHF, scaling laws — to a friend in under a minute.
